---
title: "Sustainability"
---

AEIS is committed to environmental sustainability. As a group, we aim to minimise the environmental impact of aviation using computational methods, so it is important to us to ensure the environmental benefits of producing our research (such as improvements in technology and changes in policy) outweigh the negative environmental impacts. For this reason, we have guidelines for AEIS group members to follow in the most relevant areas: [Computation](#computation), [Reuse, Repair, Recycle (RRR)](#rrr-policy), and [Travel](#travel).

Contact the current AEIS group Sustainability lead if you have any questions (see [JLT](about.qmd#jlt)). It is the Sustainability lead's role to develop, disseminate, and encourage sustainable practices in the group and to pursue sustainability accreditation.

# Computation

Computation, particularly HPC, and data storage can have a substantial impact, but we don't want to limit the quality of research we produce. For this reason, we have developed a set of [best practices](#best-practices) and we are pursuing [Green DiSC](#green-disc) certification.

If you are interested in learning more about computational sustainability, take Imperial's [Digital Research Sustainability training](https://imperialcollegelondon.github.io/digital_research_sustainability_training/), the [Green Software Foundation's course](https://learn.greensoftware.foundation/), and the [SPARKHub Digital Research Infrastructure course](https://sdratraining.sparkhub.eu/).

## Best practices

These best practices have been developed by us for the AEIS group, but they align closely with Imperial's [Seven Steps to ICT Sustainability](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/admin-services/ict/about-ict/sustainability/seven-steps/). If you have suggestions for tips to be added to this list, contact the Sustainability lead!

### Don't replace devices unless necessary

Use your devices for longer. Even delaying a laptop upgrade for 1 or 2 years has an impact. Also, if your device breaks, try to get it repaired and source used or refurbished devices where possible.

### Optimise your code

If you've written some code which is computationally demanding or that you'll run for a long time, spend some time trying to make it more efficient. A more efficient program also means you get your results faster and can add up in the long term! GenAI models can be helpful for this.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## The Jevons paradox: Greater efficiency → greater consumption?

[The Jevons paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jevons_paradox) is the phenomenon whereby increasing the efficiency of a resource's use increases the overall consumption of the resource. It has been seen observed for more than a century in various fields such as the increase in efficiency of coal use which made coal more attractive as a fuel and so increased its consumption. In your work, don't let the improved efficiency of your code be an excuse for running it unnecessarily!
:::

### Debug on a small scale

When you've written a new model or some complex new code, you should debug it on a small scale before attempting to run it fully.

**Compile with debug flags** (for compiled code). Search for the options available for your compiler. For example, GCC users can use [this page](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Debugging-Options.html). CMake has cross-platform default flags which it uses when you use the argument `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug`, but you can also customise them with `set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG [YOUR FLAGS])`. Other build platforms typically have debug options built in.

**Test your code on a subset of input data** when you first run it. This way, you won't waste resources and energy finding the same bugs.

**Profile your code** to pinpoint bottlenecks with tools such as [cProfile](https://docs.python.org/3/library/profile.html), [py-spy](https://github.com/benfred/py-spy), and [perf](https://perfwiki.github.io/main/). Add these tools into your workflow early so it feels natural and easy to do every time you need it.

**Use a debugger** if things are going wrong in your tests. Debuggers like [GDB](https://sourceware.org/gdb/) and [Valgrind](https://valgrind.org/) can be lifesavers in identifying segmentation faults, memory corruption, and fatal errors. You can set breakpoints and check the value of variables during runtime.

Once you've done this, you'll be ready to scale up with confidence.

### Request the resources you need

This applies to people using HPC platforms. It can be hard to know the resource needs of your code before you first run it, but once you have run it successfully, you can find out what resources it uses in the job logs (CPU percentage, memory usage, and runtime). Use this information to update your requests for the next time.

### Only run simulations and data analysis once

It can be tempting to make small changes to models, pipelines, or data analysis which mean you need to run computationally expensive code again. Instead, consider carefully whether your code is finished before you run it and test your code on a small amount of data first to check it works. There are often things you'll remember or discover which mean you don't have to rerun expensive code.

### Only store the data you need

It's easy to let data pile up which you don't need to keep. As a reference, storing 1 TB of data on the cloud consumes an estimated 40 to 70 kWh per year which is equivalent to running a modern refrigerator for an entire month (see [1](https://www.ecoflow.com/us/blog/energy-cost-cloud-storage) and [2](https://greenly.earth/en-gb/blog/industries/what-is-the-carbon-footprint-of-data-storage)).

Where possible, don't store preprocessed data when you have already processed the results and avoid storing multiple copies of the same data. If someone else uses the same data, share a single copy with them which you can both read from.

There are lots of tools which can help you identify data to delete such as [WizTree](https://diskanalyzer.com/download) on Windows and the `du` command on Linux. For a cross-platform tool designed for saving storage space, see [fss](https://github.com/jcbart/fss).

AEIS runs quarterly [data storage cleaning](induction.qmd#data-storage-cleaning) to encourage good practice.

### Calculate your computational carbon footprint

The [Green Algorithms](https://www.green-algorithms.org/) calculator compares the carbon footprint of your code to tree-months of carbon sequestration, kilometres in a car, and fraction of a flight. It can help to have a reference point for the computational work you do so that we better understand the impact we're having. Give it a try with the details of a job you've run.

### GenAI

Generative AI (GenAI) is an invaluable tool to many of us. It is particularly useful for optimising your code. Its environmental impact will vary depending on how you use it. As it becomes easier to quantify on an individual level, we may develop guidance on how to use GenAI effectively and how to account for its environmental impact in the future.

In the meantime, try experimenting with the Green Software Foundation's [Agentic AI Cost & Carbon Explorer](https://green-software-foundation.github.io/reference-implementations/tools/gsf/agentic-ai-impact-explorer/).

## Green DiSC

[Green DiSC](https://www.software.ac.uk/GreenDiSC) (Digital Sustainability Certification) is an open-access scheme led by the University of Cambridge. It is designed to encourage people working in research to consider and minimise their computational environmental impact. It has three targets: research groups, research computing infrastructure teams, and central teams, of which the first is relevant to us. The certification has (or will have) three levels: Bronze, Silver, and Gold.

Its priorities for research groups are:

- Purchasing and e-waste policies
- Computing hardware and infrastructure inventory
- Computational resource use
- Dataset inventory and regular data storage cleaning
- Knowledge amongst group members of best practices for computational sustainability (see [Best practices](#best-practices)!)

Timeline:

- July 2026: Jack Bartlett enrolled AEIS with Green DiSC.
- November 2026: Apply for Green DiSC Bronze certification.

Seb is the group's Green DiSC representative, but the Sustainability lead and deputy are in charge of pursuing the certification.

Useful links:

- [Green DiSC homepage](https://www.software.ac.uk/GreenDiSC)
- [Green DiSC GitHub](https://github.com/Cambridge-Sustainable-Computing-Lab/greenDiSC)
- [Green Algorithms](https://www.green-algorithms.org/)

# RRR policy

This is a summary of AEIS's Reuse, Repair, Recycle (RRR) policy. The full policy can be found in the JLT channel on Teams.

This RRR guideline outlines what Imperial as a whole, the Aeronautics department, and we as the AEIS group do with computing hardware that is spare, broken, or needs to be disposed of. We will follow existing university or department-wide guidelines except where we believe we can improve upon what currently exists, or where we think a procedure could be made more bespoke for our group. In these cases, we will specify details in our AEIS procedures.

**The takeaway:** The most important thing you can do when hardware breaks, or you're leaving, or you don't need it any longer is to tell the AEIS Sustainability lead or report it using another procedure below. It makes everyone's life easier and our campus more sustainable if devices aren't left on the side for someone else to clean up.

## Imperial RRR procedures

- Reuse: Warp It lets staff give away equipment to others internally (Imperial) and externally (other universities). However, while the Warp It page says electrical items can't go on the listings, the Waste Streams page says they can. We have also observed electrical equipment in the Warp It listings. So, we will check with Imperial Property Division to get clarification.
- Recycle: ICT partners with Converge and Academia to refurbish where they can, but otherwise recycle equipment. They both have a zero landfill promise and provide a certificate of disposal. Depending on the age and condition, they offer to offset against the cost of new devices or services. Through the Property Division's Report or Request portal, an approved contractor can also, using an approved contractor for a small fee, help to recycle or dispose of IT electrical equipment. It requires the asset number or serial number of the item to be dispose of.
- Repair: ICT-managed laptops have 5-year warranties. This means broken laptops within those warranty periods should go to ICT Service Desk first for repair.

## Department RRR procedures

While there is currently no formal RRR departmental policy, as they are in the process of formulating it, the following are the current interim procedures.

- Reuse/repair and recycle: departmental professional services staff (currently Clodagh and Lisa) periodically collate unused computing equipment from the PhD/postdoc rooms. If you have something to be repaired or recycled, make things easy by informing them you have something to be collected. The Head of Technical Operations and Safety (Nigel) then reuses some of it to fix laboratory computers, with the rest sent to the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) process.

## AEIS RRR procedures

- Inventory: all electrical equipment owned by the group is on the group hardware inventory, with its asset or serial number denoted. This inventory is repeated quarterly.
- Reuse: if you are leaving the college or you don't need a device any longer, tell the AEIS Sustainability lead! Electrical items will be reused inside the group first, so spare working equipment goes into the group pool (exact location to be agreed) and gets marked as spare, with a separate tab on the inventory database to show this equipment is available. Anyone who needs a laptop, monitor, keyboard, drive, etc. including new starters can check the list. New starters will also be required to ask in our group Teams channel if there are any spare computing hardware before buying anything new. Group leavers will hand equipment back to the Sustainability lead or the group PI, so as not to leave equipment in the office. If no one in the group claims the spare equipment after about a month, it gets passed on in the following order: i) Aero for department reuse, ii) Imperial-wide reuse ICT partners (Converge, Academia, Warp It if allowed), ii) Recycling (see below).
- Recycling: this is the last resort option, again through ICT’s partners or the Property Division. This will be done on a half-yearly basis to save items up into one request to keep fees and number of collections down. No electrical equipment should ever go into the general waste.
- Residual data: before leavers return equipment, any important data is backed up before devices are wiped.
- Equipment monitoring: every time an item leaves or moves from one person to another, the Sustainability lead writes in the inventory the date and where or to whom it was sent, which will serve as evidence that this process is being followed.

# Travel

Travelling to share our research with and to learn from others is integral to AEIS, but we should still consider the impact of our travel and how to minimise it where we can. We often travel to the same conferences and events as each other and each year. If you find a sustainable travel option for a particular destination, share it with the group!

Imperial has a [sustainable travel policy](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/sustainability/our-campuses/sustainable-travel/) containing most of this information. Section labels in parentheses below refer to this document.

There is also a Postgraduate Sustainable Travel Fund which can help fund more sustainable travel which is often more expensive. You can find details on [this page](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/sustainability/our-campuses/sustainable-travel/).

Steps to consider before travelling:

1. **Do I need to travel there?**

    Would I benefit a similar amount by joining the event online? ([Section A 1](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/sustainability/our-campuses/sustainable-travel/))

2. **Can I combine multiple trips into one by travelling between events or by taking a well deserved holiday at my destination?** ([Section A 3](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/sustainability/our-campuses/sustainable-travel/))

3. **Can I get there in a more sustainable way?**

    Train journeys may be more expensive than flying, but their CO2 emissions are considerably lower. Imperial's [Postgraduate Sustainable Travel Fund](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/sustainability/our-campuses/sustainable-travel/) can help PhD students with the higher cost of train travel. For some journeys, train travel will take longer, but factoring in travel and waiting times on either side may make up for it, plus you can work during them. The College permits taking higher class rail travel to enable you to work more effectively ([Section B 1.3](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/sustainability/our-campuses/sustainable-travel/)). The College prohibits flying domestically in the UK if the destination can be reached within 5 hours by train except in extenuating circumstances ([Section B 1.2](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/sustainability/our-campuses/sustainable-travel/)).

4. **If I have to fly, can I fly non-stop even if it's more expensive?** ([Section B 2.2](https://www.imperial.ac.uk/sustainability/our-campuses/sustainable-travel/))

5. **Can I fly in the morning so that the cooling effect of any resulting contrails is strongest ~~and so I can take pretty photos of them~~?**

As of 2026, Imperial is considering a policy on carbon offsetting for travel, but nothing has yet been implemented.
